p.courtType: IN THE COURT OF APPEAL (CRIMINAL DIVISION)

td.p: ON APPEAL FROM THE CROWN COURT AT SWANSEA

p.span: Computer Aided Transcript of Epiq Europe Ltd,
Lower Ground, 46 Chancery Lane, London WC2A 1JE
Tel No: 020 7404 1400; Email: rcj@epiqglobal.co.uk (Official Shorthand Writers to the Court)
Mr Daniel Griffiths appeared on behalf of the Appellant

content.p: With the leave of the single judge, the appellant appeals against sentence on the sole basis that an error occurred in the calculation of the credit for his plea of guilty.

On 17 May 2024, in the Crown Court at Swansea, the appellant pleaded guilty to two offences of being concerned in the supply of class A drugs (cocaine and crack cocaine) and one similar offence of class B (cannabis). On 4 June 2024, having pleaded guilty before Swansea Magistrates Court, the appellant was committed for sentence for an offence of dangerous driving and offences of driving without a test certificate, without insurance, and without a licence. On 21 June 2024, the appellant was sentenced to a total period of 45 months for the drug offences and to a consecutive term of 9 months for the dangerous driving offence; no separate penalty was imposed on the other driving related offences, but the appellant was also disqualified from driving for a period of 63 months, stated to comprise a disqualification period of 36 months and an extension period of 27 months; an extended test was also ordered.

By grounds of appeal settled by his solicitor advocate, the appellant sought leave to appeal against sentence, largely focusing on the term imposed for the drug offences. The single judge refused leave on the proposed grounds of appeal but identified an error relating to a separate point arising from the sentence for the dangerous driving: having accepted that the appellant had entered his guilty plea for this offence at the earliest opportunity, the Recorder had stated that he would be due one-third credit for plea; when, however, subsequently reducing the term, a reduction of one quarter was applied. The appellant has not sought to renew his application for leave in respect of the other grounds and this matter thus comes before us solely on the question whether an error of principle arose relating to the calculation of credit for plea such that the term imposed for the dangerous driving offence was manifestly excessive. In addition, however, the Registrar has raised a question relating to the driving disqualification, which we will go on to address below.
Given the limited scope of this appeal, we can take the facts fairly shortly.

The drug offences relate to a drugs line run by the appellant and his cousin (and co-defendant) Keeln Montanari. Initially, another co-defendant, Liam Devois, worked as part of that drugs line but he had branched out and established his own network. On 9 March 2024, Devois was arrested and mobile ‘phones found which had stored the number for the line run by the appellant and Keeln Montanari, and messages between Devois and the appellant relating to the supply of cocaine. When ‘phones belonging to the appellant and Keeln Montanari were later investigated, video evidence was found which showed them preparing crack cocaine for onward sale and the appellant holding a large quantity of bank notes; there were also messages which showed they had been supplying drugs to dealers, and dealers lists, on the appellant’s ‘phone. When officers searched the appellant’s address, they recovered snap bags containing a total of six grams of cannabis; they also recovered £170 in cash from the home address of Keelan Montanari.

As for the driving offences, on 8 March 2024, just after 4:15pm, a police helicopter was on patrol following a report of motorcycles being driven dangerously, and an officer was observing a motorbike owned by the appellant which was being driven dangerously by another male. That rider alighted from the motorbike, made off on foot and was not apprehended. The appellant then got on the motorbike and drove off, despite an officer taking hold of him and telling him to stop (the officer fell to the ground when the appellant rode off). The appellant rode along the pavement at high speed, then turned left and travelled in excess of 40 miles an hour on the wrong side of the road before cutting a junction and proceeding along a walkway. The motorbike was clearly not under his control, and he was hanging onto the handlebars as it veered from side to side. Carrying out a U-turn and overtaking traffic along the centre of the carriageway, the appellant’s speed exceeded 50 miles an hour; the speed limit was 20 miles an hour. The appellant crashed a bollard before making off on foot. He was detained nearby and arrested.

On 15 April 2024, the appellant and his cousin were arrested at their home addresses in Swansea for the drug offences. In interview, they both answered no comment to all questions. The appellant entered guilty pleas in respect of these offences at the PTPH. As for the driving offences, he pleaded guilty at the first opportunity before the magistrates’ court.

The appellant was 19 at the date of conviction and sentence. He had one previous conviction for riot dating from 3 March 2022, for which he had been sentenced to a 39 month detention order. He was released from that sentence on 6 November 2023 and was thus on licence at the time of the index offending.

In relation to the drug offences, treating the being concerned in the supply of cocaine as the lead offence, there was no dispute that the appellant had played a significant role and, given that he supplied directly to street users, this was category 3 harm, giving a starting point of 4 ½ months, with a range between 3 ½ to 7 years. Given the nature of the offending, however, and the aggravating features, the Recorder considered this would take the nominal starting term to 66 months (5 ½ years). Having regard to the appellant’s personal mitigation, including his age, immaturity and learning difficulties, the Recorder determined the appropriate term after trial would have been 60 months (5 years), reduced to 45 months (3 years 9 months) allowing 25% credit for plea. Lesser, concurrent sentences were passed on the remaining drug offences.

Turning to the dangerous driving offence, the Recorder was clear that this warranted a consecutive sentence. It was agreed to be a category 1A offence, which would give a starting point of 18 months and a range of 1 to 2 years. Having regard to the aggravating features, the Recorder considered that, had this matter been brought to trial, the least possible sentence would have been of 16 months’ detention, reduced to 12 months to reflect the totality. The Recorder then stated that he would “further reduce that sentence to one of 9 months, to reflect your guilty plea”.
Having thus arrived at a total period of custody of 54 months (four and a half years), the Recorder considered the question of disqualification, stating:

“... but for the fact that you are to serve a sentence of 54 months’ detention for the offences, I would have ordered you to be disqualified from driving for a period of 36 months. That disqualification will not serve its purpose when you are in custody so it will be extended to take your period of custody into account. Because you will serve half the sentence ... in custody, the disqualification will therefore be 36 months plus the period of 27 months, making a total period of disqualification of 63 months.”
The Recorder further ordered that the appellant would remain disqualified from driving until he had passed an extended driving test.

As the Recorder made clear at the start of his sentencing remarks, although the appellant was only entitled to a 25% reduction for plea in respect of the drug offences, the appropriate credit for the dangerous driving offence was one-third, reflecting the fact that he had entered his plea at the earliest opportunity, before the magistrates’ court. That should have led to a reduction to 8 months on the dangerous driving offence, rather than the 9 months imposed.

This is not a case where there is any suggestion that the Recorder intended to do anything other than give the appellant the full one-third reduction he would normally be entitled to in respect of his plea; rather, it seems to us that a simple error was made, the Recorder wrongly conflating the two calculations he was required to undertake, and treating the driving offence as subject to the same (25%) reduction as the drug offences. It is unfortunate that this error was not identified at the sentencing hearing or shortly thereafter, when it might have been addressed under the slip rule. In any event, the single judge having identified the mistake, we consider the appropriate course is to allow the appeal on this basis, to quash the sentence of 9 months for the offence of dangerous driving, and to substitute a sentence of 8 months’ detention in this regard.

Turning then to the disqualification, pursuant to section 34 Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 (“RTA”), in the absence of special reasons (not suggested here) disqualification for a period of not less than 12 months was obligatory, albeit the court had a discretion to impose a longer period of disqualification. In the present case, the period of discretionary disqualification ordered by the Recorder was 36 months; we see no reason to interfere with that decision.

Given, however, that this disqualification was to be imposed in circumstances in which the appellant had been sentenced to an immediate custodial term, an extended period of disqualification was also required pursuant to sections 35A and 35B RTA.

Section 35A RTA applies where a person is convicted of an offence for which the court is imposing both a custodial sentence and a disqualification (in the present case, the offence of dangerous driving); in such a case an extended period of disqualification is to be imposed of one half of the custodial term (see section 35A(4)); in the present case, that will now be 4 months.

Where, however, other offences are involved – that is, the total immediate custodial term also includes offences which would not have led to a driving disqualification (here, the drug offences) – section 35B comes into play, requiring the court to have regard, if and to the extent it is appropriate to do so, to the diminished effect of disqualification as a distinct punishment on a person who is also detained pursuant to a custodial sentence, and thus considering imposing a further uplift disqualification. In the present case, the Recorder plainly had that issue in mind, but did not disaggregate the uplift in respect of the sentence for the drug offences from the extended period of disqualification relating to the dangerous driving offence; that was an error. Although we consider the intention to have been clear – to ensure that the period of disqualification after release on licence from the total custodial term remained at 36 months – the staged approach identified in R v Needham and ors [2016] EWCA Crim 455, see paragraph 31, ought to have been applied.

We have, therefore, revisited the disqualification order in light of the steps set out in Needham. The first step asks whether the court intends to impose a “discretionary” disqualification under section 34 or section 35 for any offence? The answer to that question is yes, 36 months for the offence of dangerous driving. By step 2, the question is posed: does the court intend to impose a custodial term for that same offence? The answer is again yes, which means (pursuant to section 35A RTA) the court must impose an extension period (see section 35A(4)(h)) for that same offence and then consider step 3. The extension period for the offence of dangerous driving is, given our decision on the appeal, 4 months. By step 3, it is asked whether the court intends to impose a custodial term for another offence (which is longer or consecutive). Again the answer is yes, and it is then necessary to consider what uplift to the period of “discretionary disqualification” is required to comply with section 35B(2) and (3) RTA, ignoring any custodial term imposed for an offence involving disqualification under section 35A. In the present case, in order to give effect to the 36 months discretionary disqualification, an uplift is required, of 22 months 2 weeks. That will lead to a total disqualification period of 62 months and 2 weeks (comprising a discretionary period of 36 months, an extension period of 4 months, and an uplift of 22 months and 2 weeks).
For the reasons provided, we allow the appeal. For the offence of dangerous driving, we quash the sentence of 9 months, substituting a sentence of 8 months detention in this regard.

We further quash the disqualification period imposed by the Recorder and substitute a disqualification period of 62 months and two weeks, comprising a discretionary period of 36 months, an extension period of four months and an uplift of 22 months and two weeks. The requirement to take an extended test remains in place.
